info.title: proof.holdings API
info.description:
**Multi-Surface Proof of Control**

Cryptographic proofs of digital asset control. proof.holdings issues signed JWT proofs that a user controls a digital asset (phone, email, domain, social, wallet) by completing a challenge from that asset. Proofs are offline-verifiable using the public keys published at `/.well-known/jwks.json` (ES256).

## Core Concepts

- **Verification**: A challenge-response flow to prove control of an asset
- **Proof Token**: Signed JWT issued after successful verification (ES256)
- **JWKS**: Public keys for offline verification at `/.well-known/jwks.json`

## Authentication

Most endpoints require API key authentication via Bearer token:
```
Authorization: Bearer pk_live_...
```

Dashboard endpoints use JWT authentication via httpOnly cookies.

## Rate Limits

All authenticated endpoints include rate limit headers:
- `X-RateLimit-Limit`: Maximum requests per window
- `X-RateLimit-Remaining`: Requests remaining in current window
- `X-RateLimit-Reset`: Unix timestamp when window resets

## The 7 Proofs

proof.holdings is built around seven verification primitives. Four are live today; three are coming soon. This API exposes endpoints for the live primitives only.

1. **Proof of Control** (live) — verify control of a phone, email, domain, social account, or wallet. Endpoints: `/api/v1/verifications`, `/api/v1/verification-requests`.
2. **Proof of Delegation** (live) — a control-proven domain authorizes a typed url/purl artifact, with an independently revocable signed token. The attestation is that the domain's controller authorized the artifact — nothing more. Endpoints: `/api/v1/delegations`.
3. **Proof of Action** (live) — human-in-the-loop approval for irreversible actions, cryptographically signed; authorizations are its consent layer. Endpoints: `/api/v1/hitl`, `/api/v1/confirmations`, `/api/v1/authorizations`.
4. **Proof of Me** (live) — anti-impersonation reverse verification via trusted Circle members. Endpoints: `/api/v1/circles`, `/api/v1/identity-challenges`.
5. **Proof of Agreement** (coming soon) — continuous witnessing for group conversations; no API endpoints yet.
6. **Proof of Development** (coming soon) — verifiable development provenance via the team.management integration; no API endpoints yet.
7. **Proof of Enforcement** (coming soon) — proof that mandated processes actually ran; no API endpoints yet.

identifier.description: Optional binding check: the identifier you expect this proof to be about. When supplied, the proof is only valid if it hashes to the token's signed identifier_hash — a mismatch returns valid:false with reason "identifier_mismatch", and a proof whose hash is derived from ciphertext returns "identifier_unverifiable". For a proof about a verified identifier (phone, email, domain, social, wallet, telegram_bot) any format is accepted and canonicalized as it was at issuance; a proof of an approval decision binds only on the exact recipient value it was issued for.

ValidateProofRequest.description: Request body for validating a proof token

ProofTokenType.description: What a proof token proves: control of an asset (the verification types), an approved or denied confirmation, or a granted or refused authorization

ProofTokenChannel.description: The channel the proof was obtained over — a verification channel, or `browser` for a confirmation approved on the approval page

proof_id.description: Public proof id (ph_ctl_*), present when the proof is registered

id.description: The token's subject claim — a verification id for most proofs, a prefixed subject (e.g. domain_<id>) for asset proofs

identifier_hash.description: SHA-256 hash of the verified identifier — compare with your own SHA-256 hash to verify ownership

decision.description: The decision the proof records — present on `confirmation` and `authorization` proofs only

reason.description: Failure reason: expired, revoked, suspended (a reversible pause — the owner can lift it), invalid (for a token signed by a current registry key this includes a token the issuer has no record of issuing), superseded (the proof was verified again and this token was replaced by a newer one for the same proof — use the newer token; offline verification does not see this), key_revoked (the token names a signing key the issuer has revoked; decided from its `kid` before the signature is checked, so it does not vouch for the token — a genuine holder fetches a re-signed one), identifier_mismatch (the supplied identifier is not what this proof is about), identifier_unverifiable (the proof's hash is derived from ciphertext, so no identifier can be bound to it), or test_environment (the proof or delegation was issued in test mode, where a test key completes verifications without a real check)

suspended_at.description: When the suspension began — present only with reason `suspended`

revoked_at.description: When the proof was revoked (only present when reason is "revoked")

revoked_reason.description: Reason for revocation (only present when reason is "revoked")

token_type.description: Present ONLY when the submitted token is a delegation (m-delegation-verifier-ref). Its absence means the answer is about a verification/decision proof and the `verification` block applies.

principal.description: The domain whose controller authorized the artifact

delegate.description: Canonical artifact identifier. Compare this byte-for-byte with the artifact identity you resolved INDEPENDENTLY — a published token is a bearer artifact, so comparing it against a field of the same card proves nothing.

scope.description: Deprecated. Delegation schema 2.0 carries no scope; this array stays for the SDKs released before it: the scope a delegation issued before schema 2.0 was stored with, otherwise empty. Removed in the next major version.

control_proof.description: Public handle of the domain control proof this delegation rests on

delegation.description: Delegation claim set, present when a valid delegation token was submitted. The attestation is domain authorization of the artifact — NOT that the artifact is safe, audited or endorsed.

ValidateProofResponse.description: Proof validation result. Returns verification details when valid, or reason/message when invalid. A DELEGATION token answers with `token_type: "delegation"` and the `delegation` block instead of `verification`; its status resolves the cascade down to the domain control proof, which neither the status list (it packs each row's own bit) nor an offline signature check can show. Delegation-specific reasons: `unknown_delegation` (no registry record — delegations are minted fail-closed, so this is invalid, not merely unresolvable), `unsupported_version` (a delegation token of a schema major the issuer no longer accepts — 1.x after 2.0; its owner re-issues it), `test_environment` (a delegation issued in test mode), `status_unavailable`, and `identifier_unverifiable` when an `identifier` binding is requested for a delegation.

outcome.description: Set to `relying_party` when your app decides, after the proof, whether it accepts the verified identifier (an allow list, a plan, any rule of yours). The bot then holds its chat reply after a Telegram or WhatsApp proof until you call `POST /verification-requests/{id}/assets/{assetIndex}/outcome`, and sends the success message or the `verification_refused` template accordingly. The completion webhook and this request's reads report the completion at once, as for any request. Omitted: the chat reply is sent at completion, as before.

outcome_timeout_seconds.description: The longest the chat reply waits for your outcome, in seconds (3-15, default 10). A MAXIMUM, not a delay: the reply goes out as soon as you answer. With no answer in time the person gets a neutral "Verified. Return to <business> to continue." and the asset's outcome reads `timed_out`. Only with `outcome: 'relying_party'`; sent without it, the request is refused `400 validation_error`.

is_expiring_soon.description: Whether this request is close enough to `expires_at` to act on — and the WINDOW depends on which side of the request is reading, so one row can honestly answer differently on two surfaces. Read `next_action.role` to know which answer you have. For a `requester` the window is the lesser of 24h and HALF the request's own lifetime, so a just-created short-lived request is NOT "expiring soon" (advising a reminder before the recipient has had any time is the case this excludes). For a `recipient` the window is a flat 24h, because they already hold the link and what matters is the deadline itself.

computed_state.description: Additive machine-readable effective state: re-derives expiry from expires_at (never trusts the stored status). BOTH `is_expiring_soon` and `next_action` are role-aware — `next_action.role` says which side this envelope was computed for, and the two fields are consistent within it. Present only on authenticated owner/requester and recipient responses; absent on public/third-party surfaces.

profile_id.description: The sub-account whose event it was. Null for an account-level event, and for deliveries recorded before #421.

endpoint_id.description: The webhook endpoint it was sent to. Null for a request's `callback_url` and for a delivery to the account's settings webhook URL before the switch-over to endpoints.

profile_id.description: The sub-account whose event it was. Null for an account-level event, and for deliveries recorded before #421.

payload.description: The event body as stored. Every `proof_token` in it is null: the body POSTed to the receiver carries the token, read from its record at send time, and delivery history keeps no copy.

token_omitted_reason.description: Why the last send carried `proof_token: null`. Every attempt, the first included, sends the token the delivery was queued with, or null: a retried delivery carries the same `proof_token` as the first attempt or `proof_token: null`, never a different token. `source_gone`: the record holding the token no longer exists, or (for a delivery stored before tokens were left out of history) could not be identified. `token_absent`: it holds no token, or there was none when the delivery was queued. `token_changed`: its token is no longer the one the delivery was queued with (re-issued or changed since). Null when every token was sent. Absent from an API that predates it.

delivery_rate.description: Delivered share of all deliveries, a percentage with one decimal and a `%` sign; `0%` when there are none

recent_failures_24h.description: Failed deliveries last updated in the past 24 hours

TwoFAActionType.description: Action type requiring 2FA. Destructive actions (api_key_*, account_delete, account_delete_cancel, phone_remove, phone_primary, email_remove, email_primary, domain_remove, profile_delete, master_key_change, hitl_key_rotate, revocation_bulk, delegation_lifecycle, plan_change, auto_top_up_change) are capped at 5 min TTL and forced single-use by server policy. `revocation_bulk` is the ONE action type for every proof revocation by the owner — phone, email or domain, one proof or a batch of up to 25, from the assets routes or a signed-in call on the proofs API; a grant is bound to the `targets` named at start and is refused for any other ids. `domain_remove` gates `DELETE /me/domains/{id}`, `profile_delete` gates `DELETE /me/profiles/{profileId}` for a session, `account_delete` gates scheduling the account deletion and `account_delete_cancel` gates cancelling it; each takes the single target id as its one `targets` entry. Configuration scopes (settings_write, profile_update, templates_write, webhook_write) allow up to 24h TTL with caller-chosen single_use. `master_key_change` gates a change of the HITL account encryption password. `plan_change` gates a dashboard session UPGRADING the plan (`POST /me/billing/plan/change`), which charges the saved payment method at once; its one `targets` entry is the plan asked for (a downgrade or keeping the plan charges nothing and takes no grant). `auto_top_up_change` gates a dashboard session switching automatic top-ups on or changing their amount (`PATCH /me/billing/auto-top-up`), which lets the saved card be charged later with no one present; its one `targets` entry is `amount_eur:<amount>` (switching off takes no grant). `company_update` gates a dashboard session changing the account's company profile (`PATCH /me/company`) once one is saved — the first profile takes none; like the configuration scopes it allows up to 24h TTL with caller-chosen single_use. `hitl_key_rotate` gates a JWT dashboard session replacing the encryption keypair (a new `kid`) of an active HITL config — an API-key caller is unaffected, and the owner is emailed about every rotation from either path. `delegation_lifecycle` gates a JWT dashboard session revoking, suspending, or unsuspending a delegation (`ph_dlg_*` handle) — an API-key caller is unaffected, gated instead by the `delegations:write` scope. `phone_primary` / `email_primary` gate a dashboard session making a phone or email the primary one. `phone_add` / `email_add` are preserved for backwards-compat with existing dashboard flows but no longer gate any backend route — the add-phone / add-email flows self-authenticate via reverse-OTP / OTP verification. `api_key_view` is reserved for UI surfaces that re-reveal an API key secret; `webhook_write` gates a JWT dashboard session creating, updating, rotating the secret of, or deleting a webhook endpoint (`/webhook-endpoints`), and rotating a sub-account's callback signing secret — an API-key caller is unaffected, gated instead by the `webhooks:write` scope.

ttl_seconds.description: Requested grant lifetime in seconds (60-86400). Server clamps to per-action-type maximum (300s for destructive actions, 86400s for config mutations). Defaults to 300s if omitted.

single_use.description: Whether the grant is consumed on first use. Server forces true for destructive actions regardless of this value. Defaults to true.

targets.description: The ids this step-up is for (1-25): asset ids for the assets routes, `ph_ctl_*` handles for the proofs API, the domain / profile / account id for a single-target action. For the types bound to an act as well as an item, the act rides as a prefixed string beside the id: `delegation_lifecycle` takes `["act:<revoke|suspend|unsuspend|renew>", "<ph_dlg_* handle>"]`, `webhook_write` takes `["act:<update|delete|rotate_secret>", "<endpoint id>"]`, plus the `sha256:` target of the address when the change sends a `url` (a new endpoint, a change of address and a callback secret: the `targets` the refusal lists); `api_key_revoke`, `api_key_regenerate`, `phone_primary` and `email_primary` take the one id. A gated route that refuses for a missing or mismatched grant lists the exact `targets` it needs in its `2fa_required` answer. The grant is bound to a digest of exactly these ids and the gated route refuses it with `2fa_required` (`reason: target_mismatch`) when the request names different ids. Omit for an untargeted action such as settings_write.

post.description:
Start a new verification challenge for an asset.

The `challenge` object withholds the completion material for the pairs whose code we deliver out-of-band — `type: email`, and `type: domain` with `channel: email`. For those the code and the magic link are absent by design: the delivery to the address IS what the proof rests on, so a caller holding the code would prove nothing by submitting it back. Every other pair keeps its code, because the caller has to relay it (phone) or publish it (the TXT record or well-known file for a domain).

400.description: `validation_error`; `channel_not_available` — the channel is planned, so nothing can complete it yet; `invalid_channel_for_type` — the channel belongs to another verification type; `missing_dns_provider` — channel `auto` without `dns_provider` credentials

402.description: balance_empty. Only once billing is live: an account that has used the proofs its plan includes this month and whose prepaid balance is at or below zero is refused new proof requests until it tops up (top_up_url). Proofs already issued keep working, and accounts billed at the end of the month are never paused. The error carries top_up_url, used, included and balance (in cents).

403.description: profile_mismatch — a sub-account key named another sub-account (it acts for its own sub-account only); profile_not_owned — the named sub-account does not belong to the account

503.description: `challenge_delivery_failed` — the challenge could not be delivered to the party being verified (email service unavailable, or the send reported failure). Applies to the two mailed pairs only. NO verification is created: the row is deleted, because the create response withholds the code for these pairs and a caller holding neither the mail nor the code has no way to complete it. Nothing is billed — a proof is billed when one is issued, and an undelivered challenge never reaches that point. Retry.

post.description: Revoke a proof token, making it invalid. Accepts the public proof handle (`ph_ctl_<32 hex>` or `ph_dlg_<32 hex>`) or a verification id — the same addresses the status, suspend and unsuspend routes take. Revoking a PROOF does not withdraw the asset, consent or delegation it is about: those have their own surfaces. The revocation reaches the registry row, `GET /proofs/{id}/status`, `POST /proofs/validate`, the revocation list and the Token Status List. One difference between the two addresses: by verification id a proof whose verification is not `verified` answers `not_verified`, while by handle it is revoked anyway — the registry row is live and would otherwise keep validating — leaving the verification in whatever state it really ended in. Reachable with an API key (`proofs:write`) or a dashboard session cookie; the scope binds API-key callers only. A CONTROL proof — a domain proof delegations can hang off (`ph_ctl_*` of a domain asset or verification, or a domain verification id) — takes the gated path (h-implement-proper-deletion, DOM-3): for a domain the account OWNS the whole-domain cascade runs (every proof of the domain and every delegation issued from it revoked, the domain demoted to `reverification_required` with its DNS challenge rotated — the same act as `DELETE /me/assets/{id}` on the domain asset); for a bare verification of somebody else's domain only that proof and the delegations anchored on it are revoked, sibling verifications stay live. The body then carries `principal`, `owned_domain`, `domain_status` and `delegations_revoked`. A repeat answers 200 while something was left to re-drive (a delegation still live under a revoked proof), else `400 already_revoked` — decided before any step-up code is spent. A handle revoked BEFORE the domain was proven again answers `400 already_revoked` and never reaches the new proof: revoke that one by its own handle. An API key revoking a control proof, or one of the account's own phone or email proofs, has the act recorded for the hourly owner digest (one digest per key).

For an API-key caller, acting on a delegation handle (`ph_dlg_*`) additionally requires the `delegations:write` scope, so it keeps the gate its own route puts on it (`insufficient_scope`). The same rule covers suspend and unsuspend for that handle: a pause takes the delegation offline for every verifier while it holds, which is what a revocation does, and being reversible bounds only the cost of putting it back. get.description: Get signed list of revoked proofs for offline verification. When `has_more` is true the list was truncated — re-baseline and prefer the Token Status List (`status_list_uri`), which never truncates and also covers suspension.

The IETF Token Status List (draft-ietf-oauth-status-list) for all proofs. Public endpoint — no authentication. A schema-1.3 proof token carries `status.status_list.{idx, uri}`; fetch this list, verify its signature via JWKS, DEFLATE-decompress `status_list.lst` (base64url) and read the 2-bit value at your token's `idx`: 0 valid, 1 revoked, 2 suspended. The shared bit array reveals nothing about which entry was read (herd privacy), and unlike the revocation list it never truncates and can retract: an unsuspended proof's bit flips back to 0. Every slot the issuer hands out is inside the published array from the next fetch onward, and a revocation or suspension of the proof ITSELF reaches this channel within one minute (the advertised `ttl` plus the issuer's own rebuild interval); the point lookups answer immediately. One limit is deliberate: each entry carries its own row status, so a DELEGATION whose underlying domain control proof was revoked keeps a 0 (valid) bit here — that cascade is resolved at read time and only `POST /api/v1/proofs/validate` reports it.

A live presented key is recorded on the session, and the user session issued when the sign-in completes is BOUND to it: revoking that key by any path ends the session, and it cannot be refreshed once the key is revoked or expired. post.description: Renew a delegation in place: the same handle, a new token with a later `exp`. Every other claim is kept, so a verifier or an installed Proof gate that knows the handle picks the new token up from `GET /proofs/delegation-token/{handle}`. The old token is not invalidated: every published copy keeps verifying until its own `exp`. Proof's own checks (the artifact lookup, its badge, `proof-check`, the delegation gate from 0.5.0) judge a published copy by the current token, so nothing needs republishing for them; a checker that reads only a copy stops accepting it on that copy's own `exp`. Before signing, control of the domain is re-checked when its verification is due or ends within a day of the delegation; the new `exp` is the default lifetime capped by the domain verification's expiry. A delegation that has already expired is renewed only on control shown now: the published verification record (or a saved DNS-provider credential) is checked first, and a domain that is not on the Domains page cannot be checked (`409 domain_recheck_required`). In test mode the domain is not checked again: a test-mode delegation renews only within its test control proof's lifetime, and past it needs a new delegation from a new test verification. Billed like issuing a delegation. Sends the `delegation.reissued` webhook (a reference, never the token).

post.description: Fired when a verification request reaches completed status. The payload includes all verified proofs with their attestation tokens. Sent to the request's `callback_url` when it has one (signed with its sub-account's callback signing secret), otherwise to every active webhook endpoint serving the request's sub-account that subscribes to it — never both.

Fired when a verification request passes its `expires_at` without completing. Delivered by the hourly expiry sweep (never on a request read) — at-least-once, including for requests marked expired on read before the sweep ran. A one-shot marker de-duplicates, but rare overlapping sweeps may deliver more than once: dedupe on `request_id`. The payload carries `status: "expired"` and any proofs verified before expiry (an empty array when none were). Delivered like `verification_request.completed`: to the request's `callback_url` when it has one, otherwise to its sub-account's webhook endpoints.

Fired by two sources with two body shapes. A HITL confirmation approved on the approval page sends `ConfirmationWebhookPayload` (`confirmation_id`, the stored `message` — see `encrypted` for what it is — and the signed proof of the decision). A verification request created with `action_type: "confirmation"` that completes sends `WebhookPayload` (`request_id`, `action_context`, `proofs`) to its `callback_url`. Tell them apart by `confirmation_id` vs `request_id`.
Fired when a confirmation is denied — by an approver, or by the system (`response.channel` `system`) on a timeout (`response.text` `timeout`), a key rotation or an archived config.

Fired when the recipient of a consent request (an authorization) taps Allow. The authorization is now `active`; an approver who is not the account owner must still complete encryption enrollment before confirmations can be sent to them (`403 approver_not_enrolled` until then).

Fired once per verification id when a direct verification (`POST /verifications`) or a phone-first session (`POST /sessions`) completes with a proof. A multi-channel group fires it once, for the channel that won; its cancelled siblings fire nothing. A failed or expired verification fires nothing. Not fired for the verifications behind a verification request's assets: the request reports those proofs in its own `verification_request.*` event — to its `callback_url` when it has one, otherwise to its sub-account's webhook endpoints. A phone-first session's body carries `session_id` (the `sess_…` id `POST /sessions` returned) — correlate the session by it, since its `verification_id` is created at completion. Sent to every active webhook endpoint serving the verification's sub-account that subscribes to `verification.completed`, `verification.*` or `*`, or has no event filter (all events).
Fired when the recipient of a consent request (an authorization) taps Deny.
